newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court upholds insider-trading law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court upholds insider-trading law.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court Wednesday upheld one of the federal government's toughest enforcement weapons in fighting insider-trading abuses.
The high court ruled that the government was correct in its interpretation of a section of the securities law that makes it a crime for a person to use confidential information in securities trading.

Under the government's theory, if an individual misappropriates secret information and trades on it, it is illegal because the person has breached a trust or duty, even if the individual is not a traditional company insider.

The justices reversed a lower-court ruling. That ruling threw out the conviction of James O'Hagan, a Minneapolis lawyer whose firm had been retained by the London-based Grand Metropolitan PLC over its 1988 takeover of Pillsbury Co.
He was convicted of using secret information about the deal to reap a $4.3 million profit in Pillsbury stock and stock options. O'Hagan was sentenced to 41 months in prison.

Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said for the court majority that a person who trades in securities for personal profit, using secret information misappropriated in breach of a fiduciary duty to the source of the information, may be held liable for violating the securities law. She also said the Securities and Exchange Commission did not exceed its authority by adopting a rule on insider trading involving tender offers.
